item.title: Anthropic’s Free Open-Source Bug Scanner Skips the Human Review
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

OSS Scanner is a free service from Anthropic that hunts for security bugs in open-source software and emails what it finds to the people who maintain that code. Maintainers opt in by opening a pull request on GitHub. Each report includes a working proof of concept, an explanation of the flaw, and a suggested fix. Every report is written by AI models, with no human checking it first. Anthropic built it after a similar scan during Project Glasswing, and says Google’s OSS-Fuzz inspired the design.

The reason for skipping the human check is volume. Anthropic’s models found over 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities in widely used software over six months, and its team could only manually review about 6,000. On CyberGym, a public test, the models went from finding under 20% of the vulnerabilities at the start of last year to over 85% this year. Finding bugs is now easier than checking them. Of the findings an outside security firm reviewed, 92.7% turned out to be real. The software library wolfSSL said 72 of the 74 reports it received were valid, and five became official security advisories.

Some of the unreviewed reports will be wrong, like an inflated severity rating, so Anthropic is not imposing a 90-day disclosure deadline by default. Anthropic frames the push as a race, since capable models are now widely available to attackers too. The same launch created a program to protect power grids, water systems and transport, with 11 partners including CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks and Rockwell Automation.

item.title: An AI Workbench Built the First Complete Map of the Sky in Ultraviolet
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

An astrophysicist has built the first complete map of the sky in ultraviolet light, filling the roughly one third that no UV telescope has ever photographed. Brice Ménard, who works at Johns Hopkins University and at Anthropic, made it with Claude Science, Anthropic’s workbench for scientists, which runs a lead agent that spins up helper agents and a reviewer that checks their work. Ultraviolet light is blocked by the ozone layer, so it can only be measured from space. NASA’s GALEX telescope imaged about two thirds of the sky in 38,000 visits between 2003 and 2013, but skipped the brightest regions, including most of the Milky Way’s plane, to protect its detectors. Ménard’s map merges GALEX with Swift, FIMS/SPEAR, TD-1, Planck and Gaia.

To fill the gaps, Claude used inpainting, where a model learns how the parts of an image relate and estimates what is missing. It learned how UV brightness tracks other wavelengths across the measured two thirds, then applied that to the unobserved third. Tested by hiding real UV patches, its guesses landed within about 10% of the actual measurements, a difference the eye cannot see. The finished map labels every pixel as measured or predicted, with an uncertainty estimate.

Ménard is careful about it. Filled sky cannot hold a discovery, and the validation reports come from the same system that built the map, so nothing here has had human peer review yet. What the project does show, and what echoes Anthropic’s earlier chemistry work with Claude, is a pattern: an AI assistant absorbing the slow calibration that keeps useful scientific projects from ever shipping.

Read More: An AI Scientist That Runs Its Own Clinical Research

item.title: Linear Superposition: One AI Model Can Answer Two Prompts at Once
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

A team of researchers has found that a normal language model can hold two different texts at once. Average the word embeddings, the number lists a model uses for words, from two documents, feed the blend through an unchanged model, and the output keeps the right next word alive for both texts. They call it the Superposition Linearity Hypothesis. Across the Pythia, Qwen, Llama, OLMo and Gemma models, each stream’s correct next word often lands in the top 10.

The effect is strongest before training and fades as a model learns, pointing to the architecture, not to learning. A short fine-tuning run brings it back using under 0.025% of the original training data. On Pythia-2.8B that cut the gap between the blend and the true mix, measured as KL divergence, a score for how far apart two distributions sit, from 1.86 to 0.27. On Qwen2.5-3B, harder words moved from a median rank of 284 to 5. Two answers from one pass could double throughput and roughly halve memory per conversation.

Sampling straight from the blend hops between the two texts, because averaging the raw next-word scores pushes probability toward words both streams share. The team’s Joint Contrastive decoder, using a small helper model to steer the streams apart, partly separates them, scoring 0.43 on LAMBADA against a 0.54 single-stream baseline. Mixing streams to get several outputs is prior art, but this work ties the effect to the architecture and shows it can be trained back. Tests stop at 512-token contexts, English text only.

Read More: Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge

item.title: Lot Vulture Turns Existing Security Cameras Into a Live Parking Map
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Lot Vulture is on-premise software that turns an ordinary security camera into a per-space parking sensor. Point an existing IP camera at a lot, trace a box around each space in the browser dashboard, and it runs computer vision on the site to mark every spot occupied or free in real time. It targets parking operators who want live occupancy without the hardware bill: a magnetic sensor runs $200 to $500 per space, and a 200-space lot can cost $40,000 to instrument.

Rather than cropping each space and classifying it separately, the engine makes a single pass over the whole frame and reads features inside the zones you drew, so processing time stays flat whether a camera watches five spaces or 150. That avoids a common failure, where a tall SUV’s detection box bleeds into the empty spot beside it. A two-threshold rule holds each state steady through headlight glare and shifting shadows. Everything runs on local hardware, so the video never leaves the property.

The free Community edition runs on CPU with a model the maker rates around 89% accurate; the paid tier adds a GPU and a 98% model for $25 a month per camera. The code is source-available, not open source: you may run and modify it, but not sell a competing product. The project is only weeks old, so the numbers are the developer’s own. Cameras elsewhere are taking on judgement calls too, like Vinci2, which decides when a wearable assistant should speak up.

Read More: RuView: Sensing People With WiFi, Not Cameras

item.title: Mistral Large 4 ‘le Chonk’: a Trillion-Parameter Open-Weight Model From Europe
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Mistral, the French AI company, has opened a public preview of Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “le Chonk” after an internet meme about a giant French cat model. It is the largest model Mistral has built: about 1 trillion parameters in total, of which only 52 billion run for any single token. It reads images yet answers in text, holds a 1 million-token context window, and was trained from scratch on 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips in Mistral’s own European data centers, across more than 160 languages. The preview runs on Mistral’s API at $1.36 per million input tokens and $4.18 per million output. The full weights, which let anyone run the model on their own machines, are promised by the end of October.

Enterprises and governments want control: with downloadable weights, a security team can run ML4 in-house and scan code without a provider’s filter intervening. Mistral points to an Artificial Analysis test that asks a model to reproduce a real software flaw and then patch it. ML4 scores 82%, the highest of any model, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra score near zero because they refuse the task. A refusal there is exactly what stops a defender from proving a vulnerability is real.

Artificial Analysis’s independent index puts the preview at 38, mid-pack across 219 models, and the live DeepSWE coding leaderboard has open rivals GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 near 69% and frontier models near 74%, above ML4’s 61.7%. The firmest test arrives when the weights land and outsiders can run it themselves.

Read More: Qwen3.6 and DeepSeek V4: China’s Open-Weight Models Now Match Frontier Competitors

item.title: Open Source This Month: Video With Sound, a Trillion-Parameter Model, and a Moderator That Reads Your Rules
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

October’s open-source releases split between large models that handle many kinds of media and small specialists. Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6 is a family that handles text, audio and video, led by a 1.02-trillion-parameter model that activates 42 billion per token, alongside a 310-billion-parameter Flash version, and Xiaomi released the reinforcement-learning environments it trained on, spanning code, cyber, general, visual and music tasks. Kandinsky 6.0 Video generates five-second clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio, lip-sync included, from 3-billion and 29-billion-parameter models that upscale to Full HD. YuE2 writes a readable score before rendering it as a full song, and expert listeners preferred that planning step by 49.3% to 34.6%.

The smaller releases show where open models are heading: narrow, cheap jobs. Google’s EmbeddingGemma 2 is a 740-million-parameter model that turns text, images, audio and video into one common set of numbers, so a single search can match across all four, and it runs on a phone in about 567 megabytes. PolicyLM-1.7B is a moderation classifier that reads a platform’s own rules with every message, returns a score from 0 to 1 for each category, and answers in under 100 milliseconds, with no retraining when the rules change.

Open models are dividing the work. The largest compete on scale, and increasingly ship the training recipe, not just the weights. Small models take the narrow jobs, small enough to run on a phone or a single graphics card.

item.title: Beam: A 501B Open-Weight Model, and Why Nvidia Reportedly Wants Its Maker
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Beam is a new open-weight AI model from Reflection AI, a US startup, built for software work like fixing bugs and running multi-step jobs with tools. It uses a “mixture of experts” design, which keeps it cheap to run: the model has 501 billion parameters in total, but only about 23 billion switch on for any given word. Reflection trained it on 23.8 trillion tokens. The weights arrive later this month; an early version is on a waitlist.

Reflection says Beam matches the larger open model GLM-5.2 on reasoning while using three to four times less computing, so a team running coding agents pays less per task. The training run generated 100 million attempts across 10,500 Nvidia GB300 chips over four weeks, drawn from about one million curated coding and science tasks. Reflection calls Beam the Western open-weight answer to cheaper Chinese models like DeepSeek and Kimi.

Five days after the launch, the Financial Times reported that Nvidia is in early talks to buy Reflection or deepen its existing $800 million investment, at a reported $25 billion valuation. One option is an acqui-hire, hiring the staff and licensing the technology instead of buying the whole company, which would avoid a long antitrust review. Talks could still fall apart. Nvidia is the leading maker of AI chips, so owning a model lab would tie its hardware to the software that runs on it.

Read More: When a Government Can Switch Off a Frontier Model, the Hedge Is Local AI

item.title: Team Human: Creators With 300 Million Subscribers Ask Governments to Slow AI Down
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Team Human is a petition campaign asking the public to pressure governments to slow down frontier AI. Launched on 4 October, it is led by YouTube creators with more than 300 million combined subscribers, including Mark Rober, Kurzgesagt and Jenny Hoyos, and organized with the Center for AI Safety. Signatures go to lawmakers in Washington and Brussels this fall. The statement says AI “is moving faster than our ability to control it” and calls for a global slowdown through international agreements. It asks for two things: guard the specialized chips that frontier models need, and get the United States, China and other big economies to slow down together under a watchdog.

This is a pressure campaign, not a research paper. Its bet is that governments act only when they see how many voters care. It points to existing support: 77,417 signatures on the Superintelligence Statement, which calls for a ban on smarter-than-human AI until scientists and the public agree it is safe, and 1,386 employees of frontier AI companies who asked governments to build the tools needed to pace the technology.

OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Elon Musk publicly backed pacing frontier development in September. Governments pushed back: President Trump said a slowdown would hand China the AI lead, and China’s foreign ministry called the warnings fearmongering. The same week, Axios reported that executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other labs are privately gaming out the backlash after a catastrophic AI event. Team Human’s answer is that the rules should come from elected lawmakers, not the companies building the technology.

Read More: AI This Week: GPT-6 for Everyone, a Cheaper Floor, and a Push to Slow Down

item.title: Claude Haiku 5.5: Anthropic’s Cheapest Small Model Gets a Big Jump
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026, its cheapest and fastest small model, built for high-volume, repetitive work such as summaries, classification, routing, and database lookups, and to run as a helper beside the larger Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. It costs about 75% less to run than Haiku 4.5, the model it replaces. On GDPval-AA v2.1, a knowledge-work test, it scores 1,620 where Haiku 4.5 scored 735. On computer-use tasks it reaches 72.4% on OSWorld 2.1 against 15.7%, and on multi-step coding 39.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 0.0%.

For prompts up to 100,000 tokens, Haiku 5.5 charges $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output, roughly a tenth of Haiku 4.5. Independent tracker Artificial Analysis puts it at 43 on its Intelligence Index and 236 output tokens per second, among the fastest models it tracks. Anthropic also halved what Sonnet 5.5 pays to reuse old context, from $0.20 to $0.10 per million tokens, which trims about 20% off most long agent jobs.

Anthropic’s new tokenizer counts the same text as about 30% more tokens than Haiku 4.5 did, so the average saving lands near 75% even though the per-token price is 90% lower on prompts under 100,000 tokens. Haiku 5.5 is also the first Haiku with an adjustable effort setting, so you can trade cost for thinking.

item.title: GPT-6 for Everyone: ChatGPT Answers While It Thinks
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

OpenAI brought its GPT-6 generation to everyone who uses ChatGPT, free and paid, and paired it with a feature called Intelligent UI that turns answers into small working apps. Ask for a roast dinner plan and you get a recipe with a guest-count slider that reshuffles the shopping list; ask about retirement savings and it builds a calculator. The interface is drawn from a library of ready-made parts by a compiler that renders it as the model writes, so it fills in rather than appearing all at once. The same update lets ChatGPT start answering while it keeps thinking, interleaving the two instead of leaving a spinner until the reasoning ends. Paid plans got it on October 7, free and Go a day later.

Reasoning models answer harder questions but make you watch them work, an awkward fit for a chat window used by more than 1.2 billion people a week. OpenAI’s own tests put GPT-6 Extra High finishing in the time GPT-5.6 Medium took while scoring above GPT-5.6 Extra High, and starting web-search answers 44% sooner. The models also inherit safety work from GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s cybersecurity-rated flagship, and OpenAI says they resist multi-turn jailbreaks better than the versions they replace.

An answer can now be a small tool you operate right in the chat window, assembled on demand rather than fixed in advance. A model that chooses its own layout is a different kind of product from one that prints paragraphs, and speed and readability start to count alongside benchmark scores.

item.title: AI This Week: GPT-6 for Everyone, a Cheaper Floor, and a Push to Slow Down
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

OpenAI brought its newest model to everyone this week. GPT-6 arrived in ChatGPT on October 7 with a feature called Intelligent UI: instead of replying only in text, ChatGPT now picks a format for each question, from charts and forms to tappable buttons, and it can start answering while it keeps thinking. On web-search questions it begins answering 44% sooner than the previous version. Paid plans got it October 7, free plans October 8, reaching all 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users.

The cheap end of the market fell further. Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 costs about 75% less to run than Haiku 4.5 and scores 1,620 on a knowledge-work test called GDPval-AA v2.1, up from 735. Mistral previewed Mistral Large 4, a trillion-parameter model with 52 billion active, trained on 3,800 Nvidia chips in Europe, weights promised by the end of October. Reflection released Beam, its first open-weight model at 501 billion parameters, and five days later the Financial Times reported Nvidia is in talks to buy Reflection or deepen its stake.

The push to slow AI down also got louder. Team Human, a campaign backed by creators with more than 300 million subscribers, is collecting names to deliver to lawmakers in Washington and Brussels, asking governments to agree on a global slowdown and to track the chips that train frontier AI as nuclear materials are tracked. Three safety researchers OpenAI had fired published an open letter denying misconduct, warning the dismissals would chill safety work inside the company. Capability keeps getting cheaper and more available; who decides how fast to push it is still open.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon: A Million-Token Model That Ships to Cyber Defenders First
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Google released Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, the first model in its Gemini 4 line and its answer to OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra. It is built for long, multi-step work such as software engineering, legal and financial research, and cybersecurity defense. The biggest change is its output limit, raised to a million tokens from 64,000, which lets the model write hundreds of thousands of tokens in one pass. Google reports 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, a long-horizon coding test, and 91.7% on LVBench for long video. Introductory pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, rising later to $4 and $20.

Most people cannot use it yet. Google is giving Argon first to vetted cyber defenders through its Fairwind Program, which it says has over 650 partners, and to its own engineers. Security firm Wiz reports the model found a critical flaw in hospital software that earlier frontier models missed. Two outside checks agree it is frontier-class: Artificial Analysis scores it 53 on its Intelligence Index, level with GPT-6 Astra, and it ties for first on the CWE-bench security benchmark at 68%.

Argon reasons in one long pass rather than exploring several reasoning paths at once, the approach some researchers call parallel thinking. Google is also shipping it in an unusual order: defenders and governments get Argon first, while everyone else waits for a date the company has not named, beyond “as soon as possible.”

item.title: Hallucination Stations: Some AI Mistakes Are a Math Limit, Not a Bug
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Two researchers argue that some AI mistakes are not bugs but a hard ceiling on how much arithmetic a language model can do in one pass. Hallucination Stations is a short paper by Varin Sikka, a Stanford student, and his father Vishal Sikka, a former Infosys chief executive. The claim comes from how a model works: each pass costs about the square of the input length, so every prompt gets the same fixed computation. They measured one. A small Llama model runs exactly 109,243,372,873 floating-point operations, the add-and-multiply steps a chip performs, on any 17-token prompt, whether it explains renewable energy or solves a puzzle. When a task needs more steps than that budget allows, the model cannot get it right.

Listing every combination of a set of tokens, or multiplying two large matrices, needs far more steps than one pass supplies. The paper states it as a theorem: if a prompt contains a task more complex than the model’s fixed budget, the answer will be wrong, following a 1965 result that says some problems need more steps than others. That matters for scheduling, routing, software verification and simulation, where teams now hand an agent a problem and trust the number it returns.

Checking the work does not help: a second model hits the same ceiling, and verifying a hard answer can cost more than producing it. The bound covers one uninterrupted guess. A model that writes out a long chain of thought or runs an offline review pass spends more computation and can reach further, though the authors say those extra tokens are far fewer than the task needs.

Read More: Do AI Models Need Sleep? An Offline Pass That Boosts Reasoning.

item.title: SOMA Retargeter: One Human Walk In, Robot Joint Commands Out
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

SOMA Retargeter is an open NVIDIA tool that turns recorded human motion into joint commands a humanoid robot can play back. Give it a motion file built on NVIDIA’s SOMA skeleton and it returns a CSV listing the robot’s root pose and every joint angle, frame by frame. It ships with five humanoid robots ready to use, among them Unitree’s G1 and H2, Booster’s T1, and AgiBot’s X2 Ultra, plus 10 example walk clips. The September 15 release added a configurator that registers your own robot from a URDF or MJCF file, plus foot-plant correction and a tool that tunes how the joint angles are solved.

Retargeting is the unglamorous step every humanoid robot project runs into. Motion is captured for people, and a robot has different proportions, joints, and limits, so a recorded walk has to be re-solved as joint angles the robot can follow. Putting that step in one open library, with the solving run on the GPU by NVIDIA’s Newton physics engine, removes work every robotics team was doing separately. ROBOTIS already uses it to build motion for its AI Sapiens humanoid. The tool reads motion capture, not video; a single camera enters one step earlier, where NVIDIA’s GEM-X estimates full-body motion from one clip.

It is in beta, and the output is joint poses, not a ready controller, so NVIDIA says to validate safety and feasibility in simulation first. The pieces now chain: a body model, a video estimator, and a retargeter take a camera to robot commands.

Read More: Skild AI’s S1 turns a video demonstration into robot behaviour

item.title: Social SDK: A Free Library Marketed as a Hootsuite Replacement
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Social SDK is a free, open-source library that lets a developer’s application publish to seven social networks, X, Instagram, LinkedIn, Threads, TikTok, YouTube and Bluesky, through one set of typed commands. It is built for programmers adding posting to their own product, not for anyone who just wants an app to open. The code is public, a TypeScript package on GitHub and npm that runs on your own server, and it even ships a skill file so a coding agent can wire it in.

The project’s own FAQ says so plainly. Social SDK is a library: it provides no hosted service, no database, no queue and no scheduler worker. Among its direct adapters only YouTube accepts a future publish time; the other six reject scheduling because their platforms have no publish-later field, so a delayed post needs your own job runner. Reaching each network is gated rather than free, through app review and quotas at Meta, Google, TikTok and LinkedIn, usage billing at X, and paid plans on the four managed backends it advertises.

Social SDK documents all of this itself: which operations each platform exposes, that only some routes schedule, and that its adapters are checked against mocks rather than live accounts. The reels sell a finished replacement, while what exists is integration code that spares a developer the plumbing, and only once a platform grants access.

item.title: Claude Code Mods: TypeScript Plugins That Rewire the Coding Agent
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Anthropic’s coding tool Claude Code now runs small add-ons called mods that change how it behaves and looks. A mod is a few lines of JavaScript or TypeScript that hooks an event: a tool call, a submitted prompt, a permission request, or part of the screen being drawn. One function can rewrite a prompt before the model sees it, block or retry a tool call, approve or deny a permission request, redact secrets from tool output, or draw its own pane. Mods ship inside plugins and install with /plugin in the CLI or desktop app. Features like the /diff view are now mods themselves.

Until now, customizing the agent meant waiting for Anthropic to ship a feature. Older hooks could run a script on an event, but they could not rewrite an event or redraw the interface; mods can. That lets a team enforce its own rules: hold any command touching production config for confirmation, log every tool call, or show a pipeline’s status in a pane. You can also ask Claude Code to write the mod and hot reload it live.

Anthropic calls this turning the agent into a platform and says it will move more built-in features into mods so the core stays small. Mods run with Claude Code’s own access to your machine and are not sandboxed, so only install trusted ones. On Team and Enterprise plans, a security mod called sec-default loads first to stop other mods from overriding your permission deny rules.

item.title: Mercury Voice: A Voice AI That Reasons Without the Awkward Pause
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Inception released Mercury Voice, a model built to power AI phone agents and voice assistants. It is a diffusion model, which means it does not write one word at a time the way most chatbots do. Instead it starts with a rough draft and refines the whole answer at once, so the first word is ready almost immediately. On real customer-service prompts, Inception measured a median 320 milliseconds to that first answer word, with the slowest 5% under 750 milliseconds, 5.9 times faster than GPT-6 Luna with reasoning turned off. The company says Mercury Voice also beats Gemma 4 31B, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Qwen3.5-397B across tool-use and conversation tests. It holds 128,000 tokens of context, runs at three reasoning levels, and ships as a drop-in, OpenAI-compatible API.

In a voice agent, the pause after you stop talking is the whole product. Wait past about half a second and the call feels broken, so most voice bots use fast models that skip real reasoning. Mercury Voice reasons and still answers inside that window. Audivi AI runs drive-thru ordering on it, Altur handles bank payment calls, and OpenCall reported a median response near 170 milliseconds in production. Launch pricing is $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.75 per million output, about $0.009 per minute of conversation.

The mechanism is architectural. Standard models write one word at a time, so more thinking means more waiting. Diffusion models generate many words in parallel, which is how Mercury Voice can reason and still stay fast.

item.title: Meta Opened the Code to Build Your Own Muse AI Gadget
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Meta published the code to build your own hardware for Muse, its AI agent. The project, Muse Gadgets, releases an ESP32 firmware and an SDK for Linux, so you can program an off-the-shelf board or a spare Raspberry Pi and connect Muse to “displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench.” Meta’s suggested projects include a color e-ink screen for reminders, an HDMI stick for your TV, and a small touchscreen that looks like a home-made Muse Charm. Each gadget needs a token to pair, and it appears in the Muse app on iOS or Android once you turn on Developer mode. Meta’s page adds that “side effects of tinkering may include bricked boards, voided warranties, brownouts, or bankruptcies.”

Meta built one too. Muse Home Link is a USB-C dongle that puts Muse on your home Wi-Fi, where it can switch on a light, control a TV, or send a document to a printer using community-made skills. Nat Friedman, who leads product for Meta Superintelligence Labs, said the company manufactured 5,000 and will ship them in a few weeks, free to U.S. Muse subscribers while supplies last.

An ESP32 board or an old Raspberry Pi costs far less than a finished device, so the barrier to trying a personal AI gadget drops to parts you may already own. Muse is only weeks old, and Meta is opening just enough of it to grow an accessory community while keeping the agent itself closed.

item.title: STAIR: A Search Tool That Reads the Table of Contents
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Researchers at IBM have built a search tool that answers questions about a long document by reading its table of contents first, the way a person flips to the right chapter. Most systems that ground an AI’s answer in a document, called retrieval-augmented generation, split the text into equal chunks and match them to a question, throwing away the document’s structure. STAIR, short for STructure Aware Information Retriever, fine-tunes a small language model to memorize the document, then asks it to pick the answering section from the full table of contents. Output is limited to section titles that exist, cutting invented citations to 0.05%. On SearchTome, 18 open textbooks across six subjects, it named the right section first 82.6% of the time, against 76.9% for its closest baseline.

That matters for anyone searching a long, organized document: a repair manual, a contract, or a company knowledge base. Instead of an opaque chunk id like chunk_0417, it returns a real heading that a person can verify and an agent can trace back to the text. There is no separate vector database, because the index lives inside the model’s weights. An independent developer who rebuilt it fit the whole thing into about five gigabytes of video memory, enough for one consumer graphics card.

STAIR only works when the document already has a table of contents, and the IBM team has not yet tested messy, unstructured sources like web pages or chat logs.

Read More: SynthDocBench: The Middle of a Long Document Is Still a Blind Spot

item.title: AI Models Stop Following References After Two Links, and a Tiny Add-On Fixes It
item.dc:creator: Kabui, Charles
item.description:
Download as PDF

Give a pretrained language model a chain of references to follow inside its prompt, with each line pointing to the one before it, and most models lose the thread after two or three links and start guessing. A Georgia Tech team tested thirteen open models from Qwen3, Llama, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 and found they reliably follow only 1.4 to 3.6 links, a median of 2.2. More depth does not help: OLMo-3’s 32-layer and 64-layer versions both manage about 2.6. The fix is tiny. A rank-8 LoRA, a small add-on that adjusts one layer while every original weight stays frozen, raises Qwen3-8B from 15.5% to 99% exact accuracy on 24-line chains, using 65,537 new parameters, under 0.01% of the model.

That suggests the ability is already inside the model, needing only a nudge to surface. The authors trace the effect to a relay: each line passes its chain identity down a short run of middle layers, letting the frozen attention heads read further up. On multi-hop questions built from invented facts, the same trick lifted exact-match accuracy from 41.2% to 97.4%, and handled six-hop questions it never trained on.

The lesson is about timing, not size. The chains are a synthetic probe rather than a general reasoning test, but early-layer add-ons also added 9% to 18% exact-match accuracy on MuSiQue, a real multi-hop benchmark. Models stop extending a chain once it passes their middle layers, and placement matters: moving the fix one layer later in Qwen3-8B cut reach from 20.5 lines to 5.2.

Read More: Attention Residuals: A Drop-In Fix for How Every LLM Stacks Its Layers
